title: Emulating XX catalysts for quantum annealing via self-consistent transverse fields
abstract: Fully-connected transverse interactions have been considered as catalysts for quantum annealing that could mitigate exponentially small gaps and circumvent first-order phase transitions, but their experimental implementation remains challenging. In this work, we introduce a procedure for emulating their effects via a self-consistent transverse field. All that is required beyond conventional transverse-field annealing is the ability to make measurements in the transverse ($\hatσ^x$) basis. We show that this protocol yields identical dynamics in the large-system limit, and study the approach to that limit in numerical simulations of the (uniform) $p$-spin model. However, realizing the protocol in practice requires us to consider a series of approximate variants, each of whose errors we quantify and demonstrate can be made sufficiently small. Lastly, we show how to map the protocol onto annealing platforms that vary only a single control parameter. Even after the multiple stages of approximation, our procedure can generate dynamics that agree well with the original transverse-interaction catalyst, establishing self-consistent transverse fields as a viable alternative on near-term quantum annealers.
summary: The paper addresses the experimental difficulty of implementing transverse interaction catalysts in quantum annealing. It proposes and rigorously analyzes self-consistent field protocols that emulate these effects using only measurements in the transverse basis. The results confirm that these approximations are highly accurate, making the technique a viable alternative for current quantum annealers.
main_problem: The primary challenge is emulating the effects of fully-connected transverse interactions, which act as catalysts in quantum annealing but are experimentally difficult to implement directly.
main_result: A self-consistent transverse field protocol can successfully emulate these catalyst dynamics, establishing it as a viable alternative for near-term quantum annealers by quantifying and minimizing approximation errors.
method: The authors introduce several self-consistent protocols (SCE, SCD, SCM) that replace the direct interaction term with an iteratively determined transverse field $\Gamma(t)$, analyzed via large-$N$ limit calculations and numerical simulations.
model_or_system: The work focuses on quantum annealing applied to spin glass models, specifically using the $p$-spin model Hamiltonian. The dynamics are governed by time-dependent Hamiltonians involving both $\sigma_z$ (problem) and $\sigma_x$ (transverse field/catalyst) terms.
key_observables: Average z-magnetization ($m_z(t)$), average x-magnetization ($\langle\hat{\sigma}_x^iangle$), and the error metric ($\Delta z$) comparing different simulation protocols.
important_parameters: System size ($N$), annealing parameters ($s, \lambda$), waiting time interval ($w$), number of measurements ($k$), and total evolution time ($T$).
main_assumptions: The core assumption is that the dynamics can be accurately captured by replacing the interaction term with a self-consistently determined transverse field. The protocol's performance degrades at large $T$.
figures_summary: Figures illustrate error comparisons ($\Delta z$) between Exact Diagonalization (ED) and various self-consistent protocols (SCE, SCD, SCM) across different parameter regimes, showing how errors scale with system size or approximation parameters.
paper_structure: The paper first introduces the problem of emulating transverse catalysts. It then develops and compares multiple self-consistent protocols (SCE, SCD, SCM), rigorously proving their equivalence to the original dynamics in the large-$N$ limit for SCE. Finally, it analyzes the error scaling of these approximations across different physical regimes, including phase transitions.
why_interesting: This work provides a concrete, implementable theoretical framework for simulating complex quantum interactions (like those found in spin glasses) on near-term hardware by mapping difficult terms onto controllable single-parameter controls.
analysis_basis: full PDF text, analyzed in chunks

figures.caption: FIG. 1. Sketch of the self-consistent protocol for emulating fully-connected transverse interactions. We add an additional transverse field Γ(t) to the Hamiltonian (orange curve) instead of the transverse interactions. At equally spaced intervals (dashed lines), we estimate the average x-magnetization (blue curve) and set Γ(t) equal to that value for the subsequent interval. Note that more sophisticated interpolation schemes for Γ(t) are also possible (see Appendix B).

FIG. 2. Ground-state z-magnetization in the p-spin model with a transverse field and transverse interactions (i.e., Eq. (2) using Eq. (8) for H0), specifically for p = 3 and h = 1. See Appendix C for details of the calculation. The red line indicates the protocol path that we follow in the numerical simulations — note that no phase transitions occur along that path or anywhere in the parameter space.

FIG. 3. Dynamics of the z-magnetization under ED (blue) and SCE (orange), for the p-spin model with p = 3 and h = 1. The annealing schedule is s(t) = λ(t) = t/T, and the runtime is T = 25. The three panels differ only in the system size — N = 25 (left), N = 100 (center), and N = 400 (right).
FIG. 4. Error between ED and SCE, ∆z ED/SCE, as a function of N (left) and T (right). The problem Hamiltonian again has p = 3 and h = 1, and the annealing schedule is s(t) = λ(t) = t/T.

FIG. 5. Error between SCE and SCD, ∆z SCE/SCD, as a function of the waiting time w used in SCD (system size is N = 100 and the problem Hamiltonian again has p = 3 and h = 1). The left panel shows ∆z SCE/SCD for all values of w considered at T = 25, while the right panel is zoomed in to the small-w regime and shows multiple values of T.
